intro.html: When writers want to say “the best example” or “the model to follow,” they have many words to choose from. Seven of these name the model itself, one describes being the perfect example, and two are verbs for following a model or showing what a type is like.

The perfect example: paragon (of a good quality), epitome, quintessential. The model or pattern: paradigm, archetype (the original), prototype (the first trial version), exemplar, benchmark (a standard to measure by). Verbs: emulate (copy someone you admire, hoping to match them) and typify (be a typical example).

words.def: a typical example or model; also, a widely accepted way of thinking
words.ex: Her neat, colorful notes became the {paradigm} for the whole study group.
words.ctx: For centuries, people accepted the old {paradigm} that the sun circled the earth; only careful measurements finally overturned that whole way of thinking.
words.etym: From Greek paradeigma, “a pattern, an example”: para (beside) + deiknynai (to show).

mn.text: Jonah leads the parade with a high-stepping march, and every child behind him copies each step. His march is the {paradigm}.

scene.alt: A teen leads a parade, and the children behind him copy his marching steps.

words.def: a model of excellence; a perfect example of a good quality
words.ex: Granny Mae is a {paragon} of patience; no one has ever heard her raise her voice.
words.ctx: The knight in the old tales was a {paragon} of courage and kindness: he never ran from danger and never turned away anyone in need.
words.etym: From Old Italian paragone, “a touchstone,” a stone once used to test the purity of gold.

mn.cue: a PAIR of GOLD medals: a model of goodness
mn.text: Rosa wins a pair of gold medals at school, one for kindness and one for honesty. She is a {paragon} of good character.

scene.alt: A teen wins two gold medals, for kindness and honesty, while friends clap.

words.def: a perfect example of a quality or a type
words.ex: With his top hat and gold watch chain, Victor looked like the {epitome} of an old-fashioned gentleman.
words.ctx: The cottage was the {epitome} of coziness: a crackling fire, a sleeping cat, a kettle humming on the stove and a quilt over every chair.
words.etym: From Greek epitome, “a summary, a cutting short”: epi (upon) + temnein (to cut). The perfect example sums up a whole type in one.
words.note: Say it ih-PIT-uh-mee, in four syllables, not “EP-ih-tome.”

mn.text: Curled on a soft rug by the warm fire, the cat purrs: “Look at me!” She is the {epitome} of coziness.

scene.alt: A cat curls up on a rug by a warm fire, the picture of coziness.

words.def: an original model; a classic example of a type that others follow
words.ex: The wise old wizard is an {archetype} found in stories all over the world.
words.ctx: That first clumsy wooden bicycle was the {archetype} from which every later bike descended; its two wheels and handlebars are still the basic design today.
words.etym: From Greek archetypon, “a first pattern”: arche (beginning) + typos (a mark, a model).

mn.cue: ARCHE-TYPE: the FIRST TYPE, copied in every tale
mn.text: Professor Edwin plays the wise old wizard in the school play, and every kid in a wizard hat copies him: the long beard, the staff, the deep voice. He is the {archetype}.

scene.alt: An old professor dressed as a wizard strikes a pose on stage while two children in wizard hats copy him.

words.def: a first, trial version of something, built to test it
words.ex: The engineers crashed the {prototype} on purpose to test its seat belts.
words.ctx: Before building a hundred birdhouses for the fair, Dev made a single {prototype}, left it out in the rain, and then fixed the leaky roof on all the rest.
words.etym: From Greek prototypon, “a first form”: protos (first) + typos (a model).

mn.text: Kai’s first paper plane flies three feet and nose-dives into the grass. It’s only the {prototype}; version two will fly farther.

scene.alt: A boy watches his first paper airplane nose-dive into the grass and plans a better one.

words.def: a person or thing that serves as a model to copy
words.ex: The teacher posted Lila’s essay as an {exemplar} of clear writing.
words.ctx: The old mill is an {exemplar} of careful repair: other towns send their builders to study how its beams were replaced without changing its look.
words.etym: From Latin exemplar, “a model,” from exemplum, “an example.”

mn.text: Ms. Tia pins Kai’s perfect poster on the board with a gold star: “Use this as your example!” His poster is the {exemplar}.

scene.alt: A teacher pins a student's poster with a gold star on the board as the example for the class.

words.def: being the most perfect or typical example of something
words.ex: A lemonade stand on a hot day is the {quintessential} summer business.
words.ctx: With its red barn, white fence, grazing cows and a rooster crowing at dawn, the place was the {quintessential} farm, just like the pictures in a children’s book.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin quinta essentia, “the fifth essence,” a pure substance once thought to fill the heavens, beyond earth, air, fire and water.

mn.text: Sun, sand, waves, a bucket and an ice cream cone: Ivy’s beach day has all five essentials. It is the {quintessential} summer day.

scene.alt: A girl in sunglasses cheers with an ice cream cone on a sunny beach with a bucket, a sandcastle and a beach ball.

words.def: to imitate someone you admire, hoping to match or surpass them
words.ex: Little Theo {emulates} his big sister, practicing her cartwheels every afternoon.
words.ctx: Jamal did not merely copy his grandmother’s recipes; he tried to {emulate} her, aiming to cook as well as she did and someday to invent dishes of his own.
words.etym: From Latin aemulari, “to rival, to try to equal,” from aemulus, “a rival.”
words.note: Emulate means more than copy: you emulate someone you admire, hoping to match or even beat them.

mn.cue: EM-U-LATE: “I’ll be like EM, you’ll see, LATEr!”
mn.text: Little Theo watches his big sister Em stretch up tall before her dance, then copies her move exactly: one day he’ll be as good as Em. He {emulates} her.

scene.alt: A small boy copies his big sister's dance stretch, hoping to be as good as she is someday.

words.def: to be a typical example of; to show the usual features of
words.ex: Long lines and loud music {typify} the first day of the county fair.
words.ctx: Red brick houses with white porches {typify} the old neighborhood; walk down any of its streets, and you will see dozens of them.
words.etym: From type (a model, a kind) + -ify (to make).

mn.text: A cactus, a camel and a blazing sun: these three {typify} the desert.

scene.alt: A camel and a cactus under a blazing sun show what a typical desert looks like.

words.def: a standard that other things are measured against
words.ex: Her record time became the {benchmark} for every runner on the team.
words.ctx: The first phone that fit in a pocket set a new {benchmark}; after that, every company measured its phones against that one’s size and weight.
words.etym: From surveying: a benchmark was a mark cut into stone where a surveyor set a bracket, or bench, to measure heights from.

mn.cue: BENCH-MARK: the MARK on the BENCH
mn.text: Every summer, Lila stands by the old park bench where Dad once marked her height. That mark is the {benchmark} she measures her growing against.

scene.alt: A girl stands by a park bench marked with last year's height while her father points to show how much she has grown.

after.html: Two traps. Epitome has four syllables: ih-PIT-uh-mee, not “EP-ih-tome.” And emulate is more than copying: you emulate someone you admire, hoping to match or even surpass them. A student who copies a neighbor’s answers is cheating, not emulating.

opts.s: Before making a hundred kites for the festival, the club built one {prototype} and tested it in a strong wind.
opts.why: A first trial version, built for testing, is a prototype.

items.q: True or false: epitome is said in three syllables, “EP-ih-tome.”
items.why: False. It has four syllables: ih-PIT-uh-mee.

choices: Inspired by her hero, Lila trained every day to emulate the champion’s speed.
Kai emulated the answers from his neighbor’s test.
The copier emulated forty flyers in a minute.
Dev emulated the trash out to the curb.
items.why: Emulate means imitating someone you admire, hoping to match or beat them, not simply copying.
Proto- means first: a prototype is the first version, built to test the idea.

items.q: Quintessential comes from Latin for “the fifth essence.” Today it means…
items.why: The fifth essence was once thought to be the purest substance of all; today quintessential means the purest, most typical example.

items.q: Type the word for a standard that other things are measured against (it began as a surveyor’s mark).
items.why: A benchmark was a surveyor’s mark; now it is any standard to measure by.
